articleTitle: Estimation of area overheads of testable VLSI circuits
publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: A method of area overhead estimation for testable circuits is presented using PLAs with scan path as an example. Parameters used in the model are derived from actual layouts. Results are given for PLAs with scan path, and for static RAMs with scan path and BIST strategies applied. The area estimation data may then be incorporated into a high level chip planning system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: Proposes Built In Self Test (BIST) as a way of reducing some of the problems currently experienced in the testing of high complexity ASICS. Plessey MEGACELL is a cell based CAD system for the design of correct first time IC's of VLSI complexity and incorporates a strategy for BIST which is simple to use, versatile and cost effective.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: TEXAS: a testing methodology guided by AI techniques
publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: Describes the development of an initial competence model which forms the basis of a Testing Expert AdviSor (TEXAS). The model would be applied to a circuit design to identify potential testing difficulties, advise upon possible solutions, and guide designers/test engineers at each stage in the design phase so that circuits can be developed with inherent testing considerations. This paper describes the specification and development of AI tools that can assess the testability of an architecture, and which can advise upon suitable test strategies appropriate for VLSI/ULSI/WSI structures such as Design For Testability (DFT) and Built In Self Test (BIST) methodologies. Also discussed are possible techniques specific to novel architectures, which are likely to require novel testing methodologies, as well as heuristics, knowledge and testing constraints that would ensure such architectures utilise silicon structures that are readily testable using realistic fault assumptions (e.g. ROM's, PLA's, regular arrays, repetitive FSM implementations etc.).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: This presentation concentrates on the fundamental definitions and then develops the main types of circuit structures that allow for easy testing of VLSI ICs. It is assumed that the testing is performed to confirm correct manufacture and not to validate the design. There are two decisions that must be made before test pattern generation can be started. Firstly, what type of testing should be used and secondly, what type of fault models should be considered? The two types of testing are, firstly, has the device (system) been constructed correctly structurally, and secondly, does the device perform the function it has been designed to do? In functional testing there is very little or even no structured knowledge of the device available. When structural information is available it should be used to improve the fault coverage of functional testing. Three different levels of fault models are often used, these being, functional blocks, gate and switch levels.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A flexible approach to test generation for scan design circuits
publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: A solution to testing VLSI is the use of a Design-for-test structured technique which improves the observability and controllability of the circuit. One such technique, known as SCAN, requires that registers can be configured so that they can be serially loaded and read directly from the device's pins. Every register is now controllable and observable allowing test generation software to achieve maximum fault coverage with a few test vectors. Scan designs typically have a 10% to 15% silicon overhead and require three additional device pins. However, with an appropriate test generation tool, test preparation time for scan designs can be reduced from weeks to hours.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An investigation of statistical fault analysis for combinational logic circuits
publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: The technique discussed concentrates on the STAtistical Fault ANanlysis (STAFAN) technique, which has been suggested as alternative to a full fault simulation. This technique uses the data obtained from a single fault free simulation, and estimates the probability of detecting each fault. The CPU and memory requirements of this technique are thus greatly reduced from the fully deterministic procedure mentioned above. The results can be used both to predict the fault coverage of a given set of test patterns and to indicate the faults which are unlikely to be detected. The STAFAN algorithm as applied to combinational circuits has been implemented in the 'C' language in a VMS environment, and the results of the application of this algorithm to five combinational circuits have been compared with those provided by a conventional fault simulator. In addition, another version of the STAFAN algorithm (referred to as STEV-Statistical Test EValuation) which uses a simplification in the technique for calculating observability values and consequently requires less CPU time, has also been evaluated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A knowledge-based methodology for designing concurrent error detecting VLSI circuits
publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: The goal of this research is to develop a structured methodology within an applicative framework to automate the design of concurrent error detecting (CED) VLSI circuits. The authors have utilised AI techniques to integrate a model of the design process with domain specific knowledge such as particular CED techniques and analysis algorithms. This paper describes the broad aspects of a prototype CAD tool PROCEDE (PROlog based Concurrent Error Detecting Expert) that is being developed to enable the testing and subsequent refinement of this methodology. The authors focus on strongly fault-secure (SFS) systems. These are a subset of CED systems whose behaviour is highly desirable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: Terminology normally associated with Knowledge Based Systems is here applied to the domain of test generation of combination circuits. Issues and objectives in test generation are discussed, and a new algorithm, implemented in Prolog is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CMOS transistor faults and their effect on logic design
publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: In CMOS technology the modes of failure of individual transistors lead to combinational logic circuits designed in different styles having very different testability properties. This paper briefly reviews the various faults present in CMOS circuits and how their presence affects the testability of two logic design styles: static full CMOS and dynamic domino CMOS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of fault testing to a railway signalling system
publicationTitle: 1988 IEE Colloquium on Design for Testability (Digest No. 1988/32)
abstract: Undergraduate students of the Engineering Science Department at the University of Exeter have recently begun using Electronic CAD systems as part of their coursework. This paper reports on this work. The paper outlines aspects of a railway signalling system and describes a case study using CMOS ASIC, which involved the application of fault testing. The design for testability techniques are discussed and the final test strategy and evaluation of the project is reported. Finally a summary of further developments, that could be undertaken in future project work, is provided.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
